source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Frames test-time compute as a proposer (the model's answer distribution, maybe revised) plus a verifier (selects or searches). Defines a compute-optimal strategy: pick the method and settings per prompt for the budget.
numbers: Setup: MATH benchmark, PaLM 2-S* finetuned for revisions and as a process reward model (PRM). Compute-optimal policy defined by their Eq. 1 (argmax of expected accuracy over hyperparameters, per prompt and budget N).
quote: In general, we would therefore like to select the optimal allocation of our test-time compute budget for a given problem.
limits: Needed finetuned revision and verifier models because off-the-shelf models could not revise or verify well on MATH (their footnote). Results are for PaLM 2, not modern reasoning models.
agent_relevance: This is the formal root of guardrail G12: allocate by prompt, not uniformly.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Difficulty is the control variable. Questions are binned into 5 levels by the base model's own pass rate (2048 samples). A model-predicted version uses verifier scores instead of ground truth. Model-specific bins predicted benefit better than MATH's human difficulty labels.
numbers: 5 difficulty bins; oracle difficulty needs ground truth; model-predicted difficulty uses averaged verifier score over the same 2048 samples per problem.
limits: Estimating difficulty itself costs inference compute. Oracle bins cannot be used at deployment.
agent_relevance: S0 gate needs a cheap difficulty estimate. The paper says that estimate is not free; budget for it.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Headline: compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute, for both revisions and PRM search.
numbers: About 4x less computation than the best-of-N baseline, in both the revision setting and the PRM-search setting (MATH, PaLM 2-S*).
quote: surpassing the performance of a best-of-N baseline while only using about 4x less computation
limits: Gain measured on MATH with a finetuned model, and with oracle or predicted difficulty bins chosen on a validation set.
agent_relevance: Gives a number for G12 (about 4x). Treat as an upper-ish estimate; it needs per-bin tuning.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: PRM search results depend on budget and difficulty. Beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets, but the lead shrinks and often reverses at large budgets. Lookahead search (a restricted MCTS) usually does worse at equal cost. Search over-optimises the PRM: repetitive low-information steps or 1-2 step answers.
numbers: Budgets up to 256 generations (4/16/64/256 in the bin analysis). Lookahead cost counted as N x (k+1) samples. Beam search showed over-optimisation on easy bins 1-2, steady gain over best-of-N on medium bins 3-4.
limits: One PRM, one model family, MATH only. Search methods swept only over limited settings (they say they could not sweep everything).
agent_relevance: Do not search on easy items. Search helps medium items. A learned scorer can be gamed (links to G10, G5).

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Sequential revision vs parallel sampling: sequential edges parallel overall, but a best ratio of sequential to parallel compute exists and depends on difficulty. Easy questions favour more sequential revision; hard questions favour a balance with more parallel exploration.
numbers: Revision model; sweep of sequential-to-parallel ratios (their Fig. 7); budgets up to 128 generations for the ratio sweep.
limits: Revision model was finetuned on on-policy best-of-N data; prompting alone does not give revisions.
agent_relevance: Supports S0 branching: easy -> one pass plus checks; hard -> several independent attempts.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: FLOPs-matched test-time vs pretraining: when the inference load is small, test-time compute with a small model can beat a 14x larger pretrained model on easy and medium questions. On the hardest questions, or with heavy inference load, extra pretraining wins.
numbers: Ratio R of inference tokens to pretraining tokens: R<<1 test-time often preferable; R~=1 mixed; R>>1 pretraining preferable on harder questions. Figure 1 bars range from roughly +27.8% gain (revisions) to -37.2% and -52.9% losses (hard questions at high R).
limits: Not a 1-to-1 exchange. The authors state test-time compute is not exchangeable with pretraining on the hardest questions.
agent_relevance: Hard questions: more tokens from a weak base model will not fix it (G12 foothold rule).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (fraction of problems with at least one correct sample) keeps rising with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude, roughly log-linear, fit by an exponentiated power law.
numbers: Gemma-2B on CodeContests: coverage from 0.02% (1 sample) to 7.1% (10,000 samples), over 300x. Up to 10,000 samples on GSM8K, MATH, MiniF2F, CodeContests; 250 on SWE-bench Lite.
quote: coverage growing nearly log-linearly with the number of samples over several orders of magnitude
limits: The fit is imperfect: curves are less exact than training scaling laws, most strikingly Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MiniF2F-MATH.
agent_relevance: More draws raise the ceiling (G12: resample heavily only where there is a foothold). The ceiling is only useful with a good selector.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: With an automatic verifier, repeated sampling beats a single strong sample: a weak model with many samples beats the SOTA agent on SWE-bench Lite.
numbers: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct solved 15.9% of SWE-bench Lite issues with 1 sample and 56% with 250 samples; single-sample SOTA was 43%. Five samples from the cheaper DeepSeek model solved more than single GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet samples at over 3x lower cost (Moatless Tools agent).
limits: Needs a trustworthy verifier (unit tests). Coverage, not selected accuracy.
agent_relevance: Where our agent has an executable check (tests, counterexample search), many cheap draws are justified.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Verification is the bottleneck without ground truth. Majority voting and reward models plateau while coverage keeps climbing. The gap between coverage and selected accuracy widens with samples.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority voting or reward-model selection rose only from 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range.
quote: these increasingly rare correct generations are only beneficial if verifiers can find the needle in the haystack
limits: Specific to Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH with the verifiers tested. Majority voting cannot pick rare correct answers by construction.
agent_relevance: Many draws without an independent check just waste budget. Ties to G10 (reasoning text is not evidence) and verification design (subfield 04).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Best model for fixed FLOPs depends on task. On MATH a smaller model with more samples maximises coverage; on CodeContests it is better to sample fewer times from a larger model.
numbers: FLOP-matched comparison across Llama-3 and Gemma sizes; the best model also changes with compute budget (their Fig. 4).
limits: Depends on budget and task.
agent_relevance: Model size versus samples is a task-class decision, not a universal rule.

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for LLM Problem-Solving
finding: Studies greedy, majority voting, best-of-n, weighted voting and two tree searches across model sizes. Smaller models plus a better inference method can be Pareto-optimal. Small models lead until they saturate; then larger models take over.
numbers: Llemma-7B with their REBASE tree search beats Llemma-34B across all tested inference strategies on MATH500. Llemma 7B outperforms 34B until 128 samples are drawn (Fig. 4). Also tested on Mistral-7B and GSM8K with Pythia 410M to 12B.
limits: Math tasks only; conclusions depend on the reward model used. Tree search needs a process reward signal.
agent_relevance: Small base + smart search can match a big base for the same FLOPs, but only up to the small model's ceiling.

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for LLM Problem-Solving
finding: Formal result: voting accuracy converges to a fixed limit as samples go to infinity. For majority voting the limit is set by how much probability the model puts on the correct answer across all reasoning paths; weighted voting uses a reward-weighted sum. So gains from more samples saturate for any fixed model.
numbers: Theorems 1 and 2 (proofs in appendix A) give convergence of accuracy of majority and weighted majority voting.
quote: the performance gains of using more samples will saturate for any fixed models
limits: Asymptotic result; assumes a fixed model and independent samples. Not about sequential methods.
agent_relevance: Sets a hard ceiling for sampling-only spend. Budget past saturation is waste (G12).

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for LLM Problem-Solving
finding: REBASE: a reward-balanced search that uses node quality to decide how many children each node gets, without rollouts. It beat plain sampling and MCTS at equal compute in their tests.
numbers: Reported as consistently better than sampling and MCTS across settings, models and tasks (MATH500, GSM8K).
limits: Relies on a PRM; fine-grained numbers were not extracted in this session beyond the 7B vs 34B result.
agent_relevance: Evidence that allocating search width by score beats uniform expansion.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: a decoding-time control. To cap thinking, force the end-of-thinking token; to extend it, suppress that token and append 'Wait'. Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on only 1,000 curated traces (s1K) in 26 minutes of training.
numbers: s1K chosen from a pool of 59K by difficulty, diversity and quality. Budget forcing with 2x/4x/6x Wait: AIME24 rose from 50% to 57% (beyond the no-intervention ceiling). s1-32B exceeds o1-preview on competition maths by up to 27% (MATH and AIME24).
quote: append the string Wait to the model's current reasoning trace to encourage the model to reflect
limits: Gains flatten at about six Waits; limited by context window. Distilled from Gemini traces. Ablations ran on few tasks.
agent_relevance: Budget forcing is a cheap implementation of a thinking-length dial for S0; see the boundary conditions in the later lines.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Comparison of ways to control length. Budget forcing gives 100% control and positive scaling; token-, step- and class-conditional prompts do not. Rejection sampling gave negative scaling.
numbers: AIME24 table (control, scaling slope, score): BF 100%, 15, 56.7; token-conditional 40%, -24, 40.0; TCC+BF 100%, 13, 40.0; step-conditional 60%, 3, 36.7; class-conditional 50%, 25, 36.7; rejection sampling 100%, -35, 40.0 (mostly 5 runs).
limits: Small benchmark (30 questions on AIME24); few runs; wide intervals.
agent_relevance: Hard-cap length by decoding control is more reliable than asking the model in the prompt to think shorter or longer.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Sequential scaling (budget forcing) versus parallel scaling (majority vote). Majority voting over the base Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct scaled less well than sequential forcing on the s1 model.
numbers: Parallel arm: 64 evaluations per sample at temperature 1; majority vote over 2/4/8/16/32/64. The two arms use different models (base instruct vs s1), so not a clean comparison.
limits: Confounded by different base models. Authors note sequential methods hit limits from context window.
agent_relevance: Do not read as proof that sequential beats parallel in general (see Zeng 2025, Hassid 2025).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Data ablation: training on 1,000 random samples lost heavily on AIME24 compared with the curated s1K; training on all 59K gave little extra. Quality and difficulty of traces mattered.
numbers: Ablation table for AIME24 shows 1K-random at 36.7; text says about -30% on AIME24 on average for random/diverse choices. Table text is garbled in the PDF extraction, so other cells were not used.
limits: Partly garbled table; read only the headline.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold-only agent only the dial idea transfers, not the training recipe.

source: Jones (2021) Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games
finding: Early train-time vs test-time compute trade, measured with AlphaZero on Hex. Test-time search compute can be exchanged for train compute at a stable ratio.
numbers: For each extra 10x of train-time compute, about 15x of test-time compute can be eliminated with performance unchanged, down to a floor of single-node tree search. Linear in log-compute.
quote: for each additional 10x of train-time compute, about 15x of test-time compute can be eliminated
limits: One game family (Hex); the author says it may not hold in other games.
agent_relevance: Historical anchor for the trade-off that Snell 2024 extended to LLMs.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: GSM8K and the generate-100-then-verify recipe. A trained verifier on 100 samples gives a boost comparable to a 30x model-size increase over finetuning, and verifiers scale better with data.
numbers: Test-time: 100 sampled solutions per problem ranked by the verifier. GPT-3 6B and 175B. Verifiers did not help at small dataset sizes (overfitting); strong boost only with enough data. Dropout acted as a strong regulariser.
quote: approximately the same performance boost as a 30x model size increase
limits: 2021-era GPT-3; school-level maths.
agent_relevance: Origin of best-of-N plus verifier. Verifier training cost is a hidden cost a scaffold does not pay, and a scaffold has no trained verifier.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Sample several chain-of-thought paths and take the most common final answer. Large gains over greedy decoding with no training.
numbers: With 40 paths: GSM8K +17.9 points (PaLM-540B CoT 56.5 to 74.4), SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2 (abstract). Weaker models gained +3 to +6 points (UL2-20B) vs +9 to +23 (LaMDA, PaLM-540B).
limits: Works only when answers can be matched exactly. Gains grow with model strength.
agent_relevance: Cheapest test-time spend: draw several, vote. Voting on a weak base saturates (see Wu 2024 theorem).

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Writing out intermediate steps is the earliest 'spend more tokens' result for LLMs. The effect appears only at large scale.
numbers: PaLM 540B on GSM8K: standard prompting 17.9%, chain of thought 56.9% (+39.0). On the other four benchmark columns the table gains are +9.6, +1.8, +10.6 and +14.2 points.
limits: Emergent with scale; small models did not benefit. Benchmark names for the smaller-gain columns were not confirmed in this session.
agent_relevance: Tokens spent on steps help only if the model is strong enough; an S0 gate should skip extra reasoning where the gain is near +2.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: Process supervision (step labels) beats outcome supervision for a reward model used to pick the best of many samples.
numbers: Best-of-1860 on a MATH subset: process-supervised reward model solved 78.2%, outcome-supervised 72.4%, majority voting 69.6%. PRM800K released with 800,000 step labels.
limits: Large human labelling cost; best-of-1860 is a heavy spend. Subset of MATH.
agent_relevance: Supports step-level checking over final-answer checking when budget allows; compare G10.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards makes the model learn to think longer by itself: response length grows during training and accuracy rises. Reflection words such as 'wait' increase.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Zero AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL; self-consistency decoding raises it further (cons@16).
quote: DeepSeek-R1-Zero naturally learns to solve reasoning tasks with more thinking time.
limits: Training-time effect, not available to a scaffold-only agent. Length rises with accuracy, but length is not shown to be the cause.
agent_relevance: Shows what a model trained for long thinking does. A scaffold cannot get it, but can emulate parts (check, backtrack) at a cost.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Extends and partly corrects Snell: the best method depends on policy model size, the PRM, and difficulty. Quantile difficulty bins are unreliable across models, so they use absolute pass@1 thresholds. Small models gain from search; large models gain from best-of-N.
numbers: Difficulty: easy 50-100%, medium 10-50%, hard 0-10% pass@1. Small models (<7B): best-of-N for easy, beam search for hard. 7B-32B: DVTS for easy and medium, beam for hard. 72B: best-of-N best at all levels. MATH-500: Llama-3.2-1B CoT 26.0, majority 39.0, compute-optimal TTS 66.2 (+154.6%, >256x efficiency); abstract: 1B exceeds 405B, 7B distilled model beats o1 and DeepSeek-R1.
quote: a 1B LLM can exceed a 405B LLM on MATH-500
limits: PRM-dependent; PRM generalisation across policies is a limit; MATH-500 and AIME24 only. Efficiency counts inference FLOPs against large-model totals.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the allocation rule must be re-tuned per model and per verifier; Snell's rule does not transfer unchanged.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend huge token counts on trivial problems; later solutions add little. Self-training with length preference optimisation cuts tokens without losing accuracy.
numbers: On '2+3=?' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; 13 solutions generated. In over 92% of cases the first round already gave the correct answer. SimPO cut tokens by 22.3% on MATH500 (QwQ-32B-Preview). Tested on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
limits: One model family (QwQ and R1 variants); the fix involves training; the first-correction-only variant lowered accuracy on harder sets.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the S0 gate and for stopping early on easy items.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink it. Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: For the same question, shorter sampled reasoning chains are more often correct than longer ones. short-m@k runs k chains in parallel, stops after the first m finish, and votes among them.
numbers: Shortest chain beats a random chain by up to 18.8 points and the longest by up to 34.5 points; shortest chains are 50% and 67% shorter than random and longest. short-1@k uses up to 40% fewer thinking tokens than majority vote with similar or better accuracy at low compute; short-3@k beats majority voting at all budgets with up to 33% less wall time.
quote: longer thinking does not necessarily translate to improved performance
limits: Four reasoning models, four benchmarks; within-question comparison. Not causal: wrong chains may wander for other reasons.
agent_relevance: Use chain length as a cheap signal; stop when the first few attempts finish.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models: Do they Truly Possess Test-Time Scaling Capabilities?
finding: Failed-replication style result: for QwQ, R1 and LIMO, longer chains of thought do not reliably improve accuracy; correct solutions are often shorter than wrong ones for the same question. Longer chains hold more self-revisions, which often lower accuracy. Parallel scaling beat sequential on coverage and scalability.
numbers: Proposes Shortest Majority Vote (clusters weighted by count and short length) which improves over plain majority voting. Detailed per-benchmark numbers not pulled this session (abstract and introduction read).
limits: Only open o1-like models, mostly math; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Contradicts the idea that more sequential thinking is always better. Cap sequential revision; prefer independent draws (G9, G10).

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: If the verifier has a non-zero false-positive rate, resampling cannot push accuracy past a bound, whatever the budget. Weaker models cannot match stronger ones by resampling.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP+ with 200 samples per task per model (1,000 for Command Light); single-sample accuracy correlates with false-positive rate; optimal number of attempts is often fewer than 10; models below the line cannot reach GPT-4o by resampling.
quote: Resampling cannot decrease this probability, so it imposes an upper bound
limits: Coding tasks with weak unit tests; the false-positive rate comes from test coverage.
agent_relevance: Counter-weight to Brown 2024: spend only as far as the check is trustworthy.

source: Levi (2024) A Simple Model of Inference Scaling Laws
finding: A statistical memorisation model that explains why pass@k (coverage) follows a power law in k. Question hardness sets the exponent. Also defines an inference loss with power-law decay in trials.
numbers: Zipf-style feature distribution; power-law decay of the average failure probability at large k; correlations between trials decay as a power law, so trials become less independent as k grows. Tested only on a simple generative model.
limits: Not validated on real LLM data; ansatz only.
agent_relevance: Gives a reason hard items have flat coverage curves; supports the foothold rule.

source: Ji et al. (2025) A Survey of Test-Time Compute: From Intuitive Inference to Deliberate Reasoning
finding: Organises test-time compute into System-1 (test-time adaptation: parameter updating, input modification, representation editing, output calibration) and System-2 (test-time reasoning: feedback modelling, search, self-correction, repeated sampling), plus improvement training and scaling-law sections.
numbers: Taxonomy figure (Fig. 2) and sections 3 and 4; claims to be the first systematic survey. No new measurements.
limits: Survey; claims not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Use as the map. Our agent lives in the System-2 branch via scaffold only; test-time training is out of scope.
